statement: Let $U$ be an open set of a four-dimensional vacuum spacetime on which the [Weyl tensor](c:weyl-tensor) is nonzero with constant [Petrov type](c:petrov-classification). A smooth null field $k$ on $U$ is geodesic and shear-free if and only if $k$ is a repeated principal null direction. So $U$ has a shear-free null geodesic [congruence](c:null-congruence) exactly when the Weyl tensor is algebraically special.

hypotheses.text: The spacetime $(M,g)$ is a four-dimensional [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) and $U \subseteq M$ is open.
The metric solves the vacuum [Einstein field equations](c:einstein-field-equations), so the Ricci tensor is zero.
On $U$ the Weyl tensor is nonzero and has constant [Petrov type](c:petrov-classification).

conclusion: The shear-free null geodesic congruences on $U$ are exactly those tangent to a repeated principal null direction, and they exist if and only if the Weyl tensor is algebraically special.

proofs.name: Newman-Penrose and Bianchi identities
proofs.slogan: Translate the claim to spin coefficients, then use the Newman-Penrose Ricci and Bianchi identities in both directions.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem on $U$, in the spin-coefficient form $\kappa=\sigma=0 \iff \Psi_0=\Psi_1=0$. The proof is an outline that rests on the cited calculation.

roles.why: The four-dimensional [spinor](c:spinor) formalism turns a null field into a spinor $o$ and gives five Weyl scalars.
The vacuum equations remove every Ricci term from the Ricci and Bianchi identities.
A nonzero Weyl tensor of constant type has a nonzero first Weyl scalar and smooth principal null directions.

steps.slogan: Write the null field $k$ as a spinor product and read off the three conditions.
steps.detail: Choose a spin frame $(o,\iota)$ with $k^a = o^A \bar o^{A'}$. Then $k$ is geodesic if and only if the spin coefficient $\kappa$ is zero, and shear-free if and only if $\sigma$ is zero. The direction $k$ is a repeated principal null direction if and only if $\Psi_0=\Psi_1=0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\kappa=\sigma=0$ forces $\Psi_0=0$ through a Ricci identity.
steps.detail: The Newman-Penrose Ricci identity for $D\sigma - \delta\kappa$ contains the term $\Psi_0$ and otherwise only multiples of $\kappa$ and $\sigma$. In vacuum, $\kappa=\sigma=0$ therefore gives $\Psi_0=0$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $\Psi_1$ along $k$ and along $m$ with the Bianchi identities.
steps.detail: With $\kappa=\sigma=\Psi_0=0$, the two vacuum Bianchi identities that contain $\Psi_0$ reduce to $D\Psi_1 = (4\rho+2\varepsilon)\Psi_1$ and $\delta\Psi_1 = (4\tau+2\beta)\Psi_1$.

steps.slogan: Apply the commutator of $\delta$ and $D$ to $\Psi_1$ and eliminate the derivatives.
steps.detail: The commutator relation for $[\delta, D]$ and the Ricci identities for $D\tau$ and $\delta\rho$ turn this integrability condition into an algebraic relation that forces $\Psi_1=0$. Hence $\Psi_0=\Psi_1=0$ and $k$ is a repeated principal null direction.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Psi_0=\Psi_1=0$ forces $\kappa=\sigma=0$ with the Bianchi identities.
steps.detail: With $\Psi_0=\Psi_1=0$ the first two Bianchi identities give $\kappa\Psi_2=\sigma\Psi_2=0$. If $\Psi_2=0$, the next identities give $\kappa\Psi_3=\sigma\Psi_3=0$, and then $\kappa\Psi_4=\sigma\Psi_4=0$ when $\Psi_3=0$ too. The first nonzero scalar exists because the Weyl tensor is nonzero, so $\kappa=\sigma=0$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the equivalence and the test for a special Weyl tensor.
steps.detail: A geodesic shear-free field is a repeated principal null direction, and a repeated principal null direction is geodesic and shear-free. So a shear-free null geodesic congruence exists on $U$ exactly when a repeated principal null direction exists, that is, when the [Weyl tensor](c:weyl-tensor) is algebraically special.

concepts.c:weyl-tensor: Its scalars $\Psi_0,\dots,\Psi_4$ carry the algebraic type that the theorem tests.
concepts.c:petrov-classification: Constant type makes the repeated principal null directions smooth fields.
concepts.c:null-congruence: The congruence is the null field whose geodesic and shear properties are tested.
concepts.c:einstein-field-equations: The vacuum equations make the Ricci terms vanish in the identities.
concepts.c:lorentzian-manifold: The spacetime is four-dimensional, so spinor and Newman-Penrose methods apply.
concepts.c:spinor: A null field is the product of a spinor with its conjugate.

source.ref: J. N. Goldberg and R. K. Sachs, A theorem on Petrov types, Acta Physica Polonica 22 (Suppl.) (1962), 13-23; reprinted in General Relativity and Gravitation 41 (2009), 433-444
source.note: The steps outline the Newman-Penrose calculation of the cited paper: Ricci identities, Bianchi identities and one commutator relation.

statement: Let $F$ and $G$ be reduced finitary homotopy functors of pointed spaces, so that $F\circ G$ is defined. The [derivatives](c:derivative-of-a-functor) of $F\circ G$ are the derived composition product of the [symmetric sequences](c:symmetric-sequence) $\partial_* F$ and $\partial_* G$ over the derivatives of the identity: $\partial_*(F\circ G) \simeq \partial_*F \circ_{\partial_*\mathrm{Id}} \partial_*G$.

hypotheses.text: The functors $F$ and $G$ are reduced homotopy functors of pointed spaces, and $F\circ G$ is defined.
The functors $F$ and $G$ are finitary, so they commute with filtered homotopy colimits.

conclusion: There is an equivalence of symmetric sequences of spectra $\partial_*(F\circ G) \simeq \partial_*F \circ_{\partial_*\mathrm{Id}} \partial_*G$.

proofs.name: Operad and bimodule structure
proofs.slogan: Give the derivatives natural composition maps and bimodule structure over the derivatives of the identity, then check that the induced comparison map is an equivalence.
proofs.scope: The chain rule for functors of spaces, with the finiteness and connectivity conditions of Arone and Ching. For functors of spectra the operad is trivial and the product is the plain composition product.

roles.why: Reduced functors have well-defined derivatives with composition maps.
Finitary functors let the comparison pass from homogeneous layers up the tower.

steps.slogan: Model the derivatives of a reduced functor by symmetric sequences with natural composition maps.
steps.detail: Arone and Ching build new models of the derivatives of functors of spectra from the cross effects of the functor. The models are natural in the functor and carry maps $\partial_*F \circ \partial_*G \to \partial_*(F\circ G)$.

steps.slogan: Make the derivatives of the identity an operad and the derivatives of a functor a bimodule.
steps.detail: For functors of spaces, the composition maps give $\partial_*\mathrm{Id}$ an [operad](c:operad) structure. They give $\partial_*F$ a bimodule structure over it, which makes the composition maps balanced over $\partial_*\mathrm{Id}$.

steps.slogan: Form the comparison map from the derived relative composition product to the derivatives of the composite.
steps.detail: Because the composition maps are balanced, they factor through the derived composition product $\partial_*F \circ_{\partial_*\mathrm{Id}} \partial_*G$. This gives a natural map to $\partial_*(F\circ G)$.

steps.slogan: Check that the comparison map is an equivalence when $F$ is homogeneous.
steps.detail: For an $n$-homogeneous functor, the value at $X$ is built from $(\partial_nF \wedge X^{\wedge n})_{h\Sigma_n}$. Expanding the cross effects of $G$ in this formula gives exactly the $n$-th term of the composition product.

steps.slogan: Pass from homogeneous functors to finitary functors along the [Goodwillie-Taylor tower](c:goodwillie-taylor-tower).
steps.detail: Both sides take the layers of the tower of $F$ to the layers of the tower of the composite. Since $F$ is finitary, connectivity estimates make the equivalence on layers extend to the whole functor.

concepts.c:derivative-of-a-functor: The theorem computes the derivatives of the composite functor.
concepts.c:symmetric-sequence: The derivatives of a functor form a symmetric sequence of spectra.
concepts.c:operad: The derivatives of the identity form the operad over which the product is taken.
concepts.c:goodwillie-taylor-tower: The tower reduces the comparison to the homogeneous layers of the functor.

source.ref: G. Arone and M. Ching, Operads and chain rules for the calculus of functors, Asterisque 338 (2011)
source.note: The steps outline the Arone-Ching chain rule, which extends the first-derivative rule of Klein and Rognes (Geometry and Topology 6 (2002)); the hypotheses follow that paper.

statement: Let $C$ be a closed [convex curve](c:convex-curve) of [area](c:area) $S$. A chord $AB$ of length $p+q$ slides with both ends on $C$, each end going once round $C$ and the chord turning once. The point $P$ of the chord with $AP=p$ and $PB=q$ traces a closed curve of area $S-\pi pq$.

hypotheses.text: The curve $C$ is a closed [convex curve](c:convex-curve), run counterclockwise, with enclosed [area](c:area) $S$.
A chord $AB$ of constant length $L=p+q$ with $p,q>0$ has both ends on $C$; each end goes once round $C$ and the chord direction turns once.
The point $P$ lies on the chord with $|AP|=p$ and $|PB|=q$.

conclusion: The locus of $P$ is a closed curve with area $S-\pi pq$.

proofs.name: Line integral for the area
proofs.slogan: Write the area of each closed curve as a line integral and expand the locus as a weighted average of the two ends.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The area is the signed area $\tfrac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$, which is the enclosed area when the locus is a simple [closed curve](c:closed-curve).

roles.why: The curve has area $S$, so each end contributes $2S$ to the integral.
Each end makes one circuit and the fixed length turns the chord integral into $2\pi L^2$.
The weights $q/L$ and $p/L$ express $P$ through $A$ and $B$.

steps.slogan: Express the area of a closed curve as a line integral.
steps.detail: For a closed curve $Z(t)$ run once, Green's theorem gives area $=\tfrac12\oint Z\times dZ$, where $u\times v = u_1v_2-u_2v_1$. Each end goes once round $C$, so $\oint A\times dA=\oint B\times dB=2S$.

steps.slogan: Write the locus as a weighted average of the two ends and expand.
steps.detail: Here $P=(qA+pB)/L$, so $P\times dP = L^{-2}\big(q^2\,A\times dA + p^2\,B\times dB + pq\,(A\times dB + B\times dA)\big)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the cross terms from the chord vector $D=B-A$.
steps.detail: Expanding $D\times dD$ gives $\oint D\times dD = 4S - \oint(A\times dB+B\times dA)$. Since $|D|=L$, we have $D\times dD = L^2\,d\theta$ for the chord angle $\theta$, and the chord turns once, so $\oint D\times dD = 2\pi L^2$. Hence $\oint(A\times dB+B\times dA)=4S-2\pi L^2$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the integrals into the area of the locus.
steps.detail: The area of the locus is $\tfrac{1}{2L^2}\big(2S(p^2+q^2)+pq(4S-2\pi L^2)\big) = \tfrac{1}{2L^2}\big(2SL^2-2\pi pqL^2\big) = S-\pi pq$.

concepts.c:convex-curve: The curve $C$ carries both ends of the chord.
concepts.c:area: The theorem compares the areas of the two curves.
concepts.c:closed-curve: The line integral gives the area only for a closed curve.

source.note: The standard line-integral proof of Holditch's theorem (published by Holditch in 1858), using the area formula from Green's theorem.

statement: In a scalene [triangle](c:triangle), the two [Fermat points](c:fermat-point), the [nine-point center](c:nine-point-circle) and the [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) are [concyclic](c:concyclic).

hypotheses.text: The [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$ is scalene: its three sides have different lengths.

conclusion: The Fermat points $F_1, F_2$, the nine-point center $N$ and the circumcenter $O$ lie on one circle.

proofs.name: Complex coordinates and a cross ratio
proofs.slogan: Put the centroid at the origin, compute the four points in complex coordinates, and show that their cross ratio is a positive real number.
proofs.scope: Every scalene triangle. The cross ratio shows that the four points lie on a circle or a line, and the scalene hypothesis excludes the line.

roles.why: Scalene triangles give $v\neq\pm1$, which keeps the cross ratio finite and the four points off one line.

steps.slogan: Put the [centroid](c:centroid) at $0$ and describe the vertices by two complex numbers $p$ and $q$.
steps.detail: Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and write $A=p+q$, $B=\omega^2p+\omega q$, $C=\omega p+\omega^2q$; then the sum of the vertices is $0$. A similarity multiplies $p$ and $q$ by one number, so we may take $q=1$ and $p=r$ with $|r|\neq1$ and $r \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Find the apexes of the [equilateral triangles](c:equilateral-triangle) built on the sides.
steps.detail: The rotation by $\pm120^\circ$ about the center $A'$ of the triangle on $BC$ maps $B$ to $C$; solving gives $A'=-q$ for one side and $A'=-p$ for the other. The apex is $3A'-B-C$, which is $p-2q$ on the first side and $q-2p$ on the second; the other apexes follow by $p\mapsto\omega^2p$, $q\mapsto\omega q$.

steps.slogan: Intersect the lines from the vertices to the apexes to locate the Fermat points.
steps.detail: For the first side the lines are $\{p+tq\}$ through $A$ and $\{\omega^2p+t\omega q\}$ through $B$; with $q=1$ they meet where $t=-2\operatorname{Re}p$. This gives $F_1=-\bar r$ and, in the same way, $F_2=-r/\bar r$.

steps.slogan: Compute the [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) $O$ and the nine-point center $N$.
steps.detail: Equal distances from $O$ to the vertices reduce to $\bar o\,r+o=\bar r$ and its conjugate, so $O=(\bar r-r^2)/(1-|r|^2)$. The orthocenter is $H=3\cdot 0-2O=-2O$, so the nine-point center is $N=(O+H)/2=-O/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [cross ratio](c:cross-ratio) of $F_1,F_2,O,N$ is a positive real number.
steps.detail: Multiply by $u=r/|r|$ and write $\rho=|r|$, $v=u^3$. The points become $-\rho$, $-v$, $X=\rho(1-\rho v)/(1-\rho^2)$ and $-X/2$. With $a=\rho^2+\rho v-2$ and $c=1+\rho v-2\rho^2$, a direct computation gives cross ratio $|a|^2/|c|^2$.

steps.slogan: Exclude the collinear case with the scalene hypothesis and conclude that the four points are [concyclic](c:concyclic).
steps.detail: A real cross ratio means a circle or a line. If $a=0$, $c=0$ or the points are collinear, then $v$ is real, so $u^6=1$. The squared sides $3(|p|^2+|q|^2)-6\operatorname{Re}(\omega^kp\bar q)$ for $k=0,1,2$ then include two equal values, which contradicts scalene.

concepts.c:triangle: The theorem concerns one scalene triangle and its centers.
concepts.c:fermat-point: The Fermat points are intersections of lines to equilateral apexes.
concepts.c:nine-point-circle: The nine-point center is the midpoint of the circumcenter and orthocenter.
concepts.c:circumcenter: The circumcenter is computed from equal distances to the vertices.
concepts.c:concyclic: A real cross ratio and no collinearity give concyclic points.
concepts.c:centroid: The centroid at the origin makes the Euler-line relations linear.
concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: The apexes of equilateral triangles on the sides define the Fermat points.
concepts.c:cross-ratio: A real cross ratio of four points means a circle or a line.

source.note: Complex-coordinate proof written for this record, using the discrete Fourier coordinates $p,q$ of the triangle; the theorem is due to June Lester (1997).

statement: If a [square](c:square) is [dissected](c:polygon-dissection) into $n$ triangles of equal area, then $n$ is even.

hypotheses.text: The region is the unit [square](c:square) $[0,1]^2$ (any square is a scaled copy).
The square is a union of $n$ triangles with disjoint interiors; the triangles need not meet edge to edge.
All $n$ triangles have the same area.

conclusion: The number $n$ of triangles is even.

proofs.name: Valuation coloring
proofs.slogan: Color the plane by a 2-adic valuation on the reals, find a three-colored triangle by a parity count, and compare its area with $1/n$.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge1$. The proof assumes that $n$ is odd and derives a contradiction.

roles.why: The corners of the unit square have known colors, and its sides carry only two colors each.
The triangles tile the square, so each interior segment lies on two triangles.
Equal areas force every triangle to have area $1/n$.

steps.slogan: Extend the [2-adic valuation](c:2-adic-valuation) from the rationals to a valuation $v$ on the reals.
steps.detail: By Zorn's lemma (Chevalley's extension theorem) there is $v\colon\mathbb R\to\Gamma\cup\{\infty\}$ into an ordered abelian group with $v(xy)=v(x)+v(y)$, $v(x+y)\ge\min(v(x),v(y))$ and $v(x)=\infty$ only for $x=0$. It agrees with the 2-adic valuation on $\mathbb Q$, so $v(2)=1$ and $v(m)=0$ for odd integers $m$.

steps.slogan: Color each point $(x,y)$ red, blue or green by the valuations of its coordinates.
steps.detail: Color $(x,y)$ red if $v(x)>0$ and $v(y)>0$, blue if $v(x)\le0$ and $v(x)\le v(y)$, and green if $v(y)\le0$ and $v(y)<v(x)$. Comparing $\min(v(x),v(y))$ with $0$ shows that every point gets exactly one color.

steps.slogan: Show that a triangle with three different colors has an area of valuation at most $-1$.
steps.detail: Subtracting the red vertex keeps the blue vertex blue and the green vertex green, so take the red vertex as the origin. For blue $b$ and green $g$, $v(b_1g_2)<v(b_2g_1)$, so $v(b_1g_2-b_2g_1)=v(b_1)+v(g_2)\le0$. The area is half this determinant, so its valuation is at most $-1$; the determinant is nonzero, so a line never carries three colors.

steps.slogan: Count red-blue segments on the sides of the triangles by [parity](c:parity).
steps.detail: Cut every triangle side at the vertices of the dissection that lie on it. A side carries at most two colors, so a triangle has an odd number of red-blue segments if and only if its vertices have three colors. Each interior segment is counted twice and each boundary segment once, so the number of three-colored triangles has the parity of the boundary count.

steps.slogan: Count the red-blue segments on the boundary of the square.
steps.detail: The corners $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$ are red, blue, green, blue. Points on the left side are red or green, and points on the top and right sides are blue or green. Only the bottom side, from red to blue, has red-blue segments, and it has an odd number of them.

steps.slogan: Compare the area of a three-colored triangle with the common area $1/n$.
steps.detail: By the last two steps an odd number of triangles, so at least one, have three colors, and its area $1/n$ has valuation at most $-1$. For odd $n$, $v(1/n)=-v(n)=0$, which is a contradiction. So $n$ is even.

concepts.c:square: The unit square has corners with known colors.
concepts.c:polygon-dissection: The dissection into triangles is the object whose size $n$ is counted.
concepts.c:2-adic-valuation: Its extension to the reals gives the three-coloring and the area bound.
concepts.c:parity: A parity count shows that some triangle has three colors.

source.note: Monsky's coloring proof, as in P. Monsky, On dividing a square into triangles, American Mathematical Monthly 77 (1970), and in Aigner and Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK.

statement: On the sides of a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$ build three [equilateral triangles](c:equilateral-triangle), all outward or all inward. Their three centers are the vertices of an equilateral triangle.

hypotheses.text: The figure $ABC$ is a [triangle](c:triangle) in the plane.
The three equilateral triangles on $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ lie all outside $ABC$ or all inside it.

conclusion: The centers of the three equilateral triangles form an equilateral triangle.

proofs.name: Complex numbers and rotation
proofs.slogan: Describe each center by a rotation of order three and show that a linear relation among the centers makes their triangle equilateral.
proofs.scope: Both the outward and the inward case; they use the two primitive cube roots of unity. The triangle of centers is a single point when $ABC$ is equilateral and the triangles are inward.

roles.why: The vertices $a,b,c$ become complex numbers.
One side choice for all three sides fixes one cube root of unity $\varepsilon$ for all three centers.

steps.slogan: Describe each center through the [rotation](c:rotation) by $120^\circ$ about it.
steps.detail: Let $a,b,c$ be the vertices as [complex numbers](c:complex-number) and let $\varepsilon$ be a primitive cube root of unity. The center $a'$ of the triangle on $BC$ satisfies $c-a'=\varepsilon(b-a')$, because the rotation about $a'$ by $\pm120^\circ$ maps $B$ to $C$. All outward triangles use one value of $\varepsilon$, and all inward triangles use the other.

steps.slogan: Solve for the three centers.
steps.detail: The relation gives $(1-\varepsilon)a'=c-\varepsilon b$. In the same way $(1-\varepsilon)b'=a-\varepsilon c$ and $(1-\varepsilon)c'=b-\varepsilon a$.

steps.slogan: Show that $a'+\bar\varepsilon b'+\varepsilon c'=0$ using the [root of unity](c:root-of-unity) relations.
steps.detail: The sum $(c-\varepsilon b)+\bar\varepsilon(a-\varepsilon c)+\varepsilon(b-\varepsilon a)$ equals $(\bar\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2)a$, which is zero because $\bar\varepsilon=\varepsilon^2$. Dividing by $1-\varepsilon$ gives the identity.

steps.slogan: Read the equilateral triangle from the identity.
steps.detail: Subtract $(1+\varepsilon+\bar\varepsilon)a'=0$ to get $\bar\varepsilon(b'-a')+\varepsilon(c'-a')=0$. Then $b'-a'=-\varepsilon^2(c'-a')$, and $-\varepsilon^2$ is a primitive sixth root of unity. So $a'b'$ is $a'c'$ turned by $\pm60^\circ$, which makes $a'b'c'$ equilateral.

concepts.c:triangle: The theorem starts from an arbitrary triangle.
concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: Both the built triangles and the triangle of centers are equilateral.
concepts.c:rotation: A rotation by $120^\circ$ about each center defines the center.
concepts.c:complex-number: Complex numbers turn rotations into multiplications.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: The cube root of unity gives the linear relation among the centers.

source.note: The standard complex-number proof of Napoleon's theorem, using a cube root of unity; see Coxeter and Greitzer, Geometry Revisited.

statement: Let $(M,g)$ be an asymptotically simple spacetime, vacuum near null infinity. Let $\gamma$ be a null geodesic with affine parameter $\lambda$ that reaches [null infinity](c:null-infinity). In a frame parallel along $\gamma$ with $\ell$ tangent to $\gamma$, the scalars of the [Weyl tensor](c:weyl-tensor) satisfy $\Psi_n=O(\lambda^{n-5})$ for $n=0,\dots,4$.

hypotheses.text: The metric has a smooth [conformal compactification](c:conformal-compactification) $\tilde g=\Omega^2g$ with a null hypersurface $\mathscr I^+$ where $\Omega=0$ and $d\Omega\neq0$.
The Ricci tensor of $g$ vanishes near $\mathscr I^+$.
The curve $\gamma$ is a null geodesic with affine parameter $\lambda\to\infty$ at a point of $\mathscr I^+$.

conclusion: The part of the Weyl tensor of order $\lambda^{-k}$ along $\gamma$ has [Petrov type](c:petrov-classification) N, III, II, I or general for $k=1,\dots,5$, each at least as special as stated.

proofs.name: Conformal compactification
proofs.slogan: Rescale to a smooth field at null infinity, track the weights of the spin frame, and expand in the conformal parameter.
proofs.scope: The vacuum, asymptotically simple case. The $\lambda^{-6}$ remainder and the types of successive terms follow from the same expansion.

roles.why: The smooth rescaled metric puts null infinity at a finite place and gives $\Omega\sim1/\lambda$.
The vacuum Bianchi identity gives a conformally invariant field equation for the rescaled Weyl field.
The affine parameter of $\gamma$ links $\lambda$ to the conformal parameter and sets the frame weights.

steps.slogan: Rescale the metric to bring [null infinity](c:null-infinity) to a finite hypersurface.
steps.detail: The geodesic $\gamma$ reaches $\mathscr I^+$ at a finite parameter $\tilde\lambda$ of $\tilde g$. Since $d\lambda=\Omega^{-2}d\tilde\lambda$ and $d\Omega\neq0$, we get $\Omega\sim c\,\tilde\lambda$ and $\Omega\sim1/\lambda$ along $\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Show that the rescaled Weyl field is smooth at null infinity.
steps.detail: The Weyl spinor $\Psi_{ABCD}$ with lowered indices is unchanged by the rescaling. Zero [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) turns the Bianchi identity into a conformally invariant field equation, and Penrose shows that $\phi_{ABCD}=\Omega^{-1}\tilde\Psi_{ABCD}$ is smooth across $\mathscr I^+$.

steps.slogan: Compare the [spinor](c:spinor) frames of $g$ and $\tilde g$ along $\gamma$.
steps.detail: The tangent satisfies $\ell^a=\Omega^2\tilde\ell^a$, so $o^A=\Omega\,\tilde o^A$ while $\iota^A=\tilde\iota^A$. Then $\Psi_n=\Omega\,\phi_n\cdot\Omega^{4-n}=\Omega^{5-n}\phi_n$, where $\phi_n$ is a component of the smooth field $\phi$.

steps.slogan: Pass to a frame that is parallel along $\gamma$.
steps.detail: A parallel frame differs from the rescaled frame by a Lorentz transformation that keeps the direction of $\ell$. Penrose checks that it keeps the orders found in the last step.

steps.slogan: Expand the smooth components in $\Omega\sim1/\lambda$ and read the Petrov types.
steps.detail: Each smooth $\phi_n$ has a Taylor expansion in $\Omega$. So $\Psi_n=\sum_{k\ge5-n}\Psi_n^{(k)}\lambda^{-k}$, which gives $\Psi_n=O(\lambda^{n-5})$. The $\lambda^{-k}$ part contains only $\Psi_n$ with $n\ge5-k$, so $\ell$ is a principal null direction of multiplicity at least $5-k$ at order $k$: types N, III, II, I, general.

concepts.c:null-infinity: The geodesic runs to null infinity, where the rescaled field is smooth.
concepts.c:weyl-tensor: Its scalars $\Psi_n$ are the quantities that peel off.
concepts.c:conformal-compactification: The compactification makes the rescaled Weyl field smooth at the boundary.
concepts.c:petrov-classification: The orders of the terms give the Petrov types N, III, II, I and general.
concepts.c:ricci-curvature: The vacuum condition removes the Ricci part from the Bianchi identity.
concepts.c:spinor: The weights of the spin frame under rescaling give the powers of $\Omega$.

source.ref: R. Penrose, Zero rest-mass fields including gravitation: asymptotic behaviour, Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A 284 (1965), 159-203
source.note: The steps outline Penrose's conformal derivation of the peeling property; Sachs obtained it earlier in Bondi coordinates.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime. The Grothendieck ring $R_{\mathbb F_p}(G)$ of finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_pG$-modules, completed at its [augmentation ideal](c:augmentation-ideal) $I$, is isomorphic to $K\mathbb F_p^{0}(BG)$, the degree-zero cohomology of the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BG$ in the [algebraic K-theory](c:algebraic-k-theory) of $\mathbb F_p$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite.
The prime $p$ gives the prime [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb F_p$.

conclusion: The map sending a module to its classifying map induces an isomorphism $\widehat{R_{\mathbb F_p}(G)}_I \cong K\mathbb F_p^{0}(BG)$.

proofs.name: Atiyah-Segal pattern with Quillen's fibre
proofs.slogan: Build the map from modules to cohomology of the classifying space, then reduce its completion to the Atiyah-Segal theorem through Quillen's fibre sequence and Brauer characters.
proofs.scope: All finite $G$ and all primes $p$, including $p$ dividing $|G|$. The outline follows the pattern of the Atiyah-Segal completion theorem.

roles.why: For finite $G$ the Atiyah-Segal theorem applies and the cohomology of $BG$ is complete in its skeletal filtration.
Quillen's computation of the K-theory of $\mathbb F_p$ gives the fibre sequence over $BU$.

steps.slogan: Send each module to the class of its classifying map $BG\to BGL_n(\mathbb F_p)$.
steps.detail: A module $V$ of dimension $n$ gives a homomorphism $G\to GL_n(\mathbb F_p)$. The induced map $BG\to BGL_n(\mathbb F_p)\to BGL(\mathbb F_p)^+$ is a class in $K\mathbb F_p^0(BG)$ that is additive and multiplicative on modules, so it defines a ring map $R_{\mathbb F_p}(G)\to K\mathbb F_p^0(BG)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the powers of the augmentation ideal with the skeletal filtration.
steps.detail: A class $[V]-\dim V$ vanishes on the point, so a product of $m$ such classes vanishes on the $(m-1)$-skeleton. Thus the map sends $I^m$ into the $m$-th skeletal filtration, and it factors through the $I$-adic [completion](c:adic-completion) because the target is complete for finite $G$.

steps.slogan: Use Quillen's fibre sequence to compare $K\mathbb F_p$ with complex K-theory.
steps.detail: Quillen showed that $BGL(\mathbb F_p)^+$ is the fibre of $\psi^p-1\colon BU\to BU$. So there is a long exact sequence of $K\mathbb F_p$-cohomology of $BG$ and complex K-theory of $BG$ with the Adams operation $\psi^p-1$ as connecting map.

steps.slogan: Show that $K\mathbb F_p^0(BG)$ is the invariants of $\psi^p$ on the completed character ring.
steps.detail: By the Atiyah-Segal theorem, $K^0(BG)$ is the $I$-adic completion of the complex representation ring and $K^1(BG)=0$ for finite $G$. The long exact sequence then gives $K\mathbb F_p^0(BG)=\ker(\psi^p-1)$ on that completion.

steps.slogan: Identify the module ring with the $\psi^p$-invariant Brauer characters and compare completions.
steps.detail: The Brauer character of a module is a $\psi^p$-invariant function on the $p$-regular classes, and this identifies $R_{\mathbb F_p}(G)$ with the invariant virtual Brauer characters. The decomposition map from ordinary characters, with Brauer's induction theorem, matches the $I$-adic completion of this ring with $\ker(\psi^p-1)$ from the last step.

concepts.c:augmentation-ideal: Its powers define the topology in which the module ring is completed.
concepts.c:classifying-space: The classifying space $BG$ carries the K-theory classes of the modules.
concepts.c:algebraic-k-theory: The target is the algebraic K-theory of the field $\mathbb F_p$.
concepts.c:finite-field: The field $\mathbb F_p$ supplies the modules and Quillen's computation.
concepts.c:adic-completion: The theorem says that the module ring is complete in the $I$-adic topology.

source.ref: D. L. Rector, Modular characters and K-theory with coefficients in a finite field, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 4 (1974), 137-158
source.note: The steps outline the standard route from the Atiyah-Segal theorem, Quillen's computation and Brauer characters; the cited paper proves the theorem.

statement: Let $d>1$ be a squarefree integer. Let $r$ be the 3-rank of the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) of the [real quadratic field](c:real-quadratic-field) $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ and $s$ the 3-rank of the class group of the [imaginary quadratic field](c:imaginary-quadratic-field) $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3d})$. Then $r\le s\le r+1$.

hypotheses.text: The integer $d>1$ is squarefree.

proofs.name: Kummer theory over the biquadratic field
proofs.slogan: Split the 3-class group of the biquadratic field, identify its dual with unramified Kummer classes, and compare these with cube-ideal classes through the unit group.
proofs.scope: Scholz's reflection principle for 3-ranks of quadratic fields. Other members of the reflection family are Kummer's theorem for $\mathbb Q(\zeta_p)$ and Leopoldt's theorem for abelian fields.

roles.why: It makes $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d,\sqrt{-3})$ a biquadratic field, totally complex with unit rank one.

steps.slogan: Pass to $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d,\sqrt{-3})$ and split its 3-class group into two parts.
steps.detail: The group $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb Q)\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ has order prime to $3$, and the [class groups](c:ideal-class-group) of $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ are trivial. So $A=\mathrm{Cl}(K)/3$ is a direct sum $A_k\oplus A_{k'}$ of eigenspaces equal to the 3-class groups of $k=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ and $k'=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3d})$, of dimensions $r$ and $s$.

steps.slogan: Identify the dual of $A$ with a group of Kummer classes over $K$.
steps.detail: The field $K$ contains the cube roots of unity, which generate the [cyclotomic field](c:cyclotomic-field) $\mathbb Q(\zeta_3)$. By class field theory and Kummer theory, $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mu_3)$ is the group $\mathcal H$ of classes $\alpha\in K^*/K^{*3}$ with $K(\sqrt[3]\alpha)/K$ unramified. Such $\alpha$ satisfy $(\alpha)=\mathfrak a^3$.

steps.slogan: Swap the two eigenspaces through the cyclotomic character.
steps.detail: The Kummer pairing is Galois equivariant up to the character of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, and this character times that of $k'$ is that of $k$. So $\dim\mathcal H_k=s$ and $\dim\mathcal H_{k'}=r$, where $\mathcal H_\chi$ is the $\chi$-eigenspace.

steps.slogan: Count the classes whose ideal is a cube, using the unit group.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal V=\{\alpha:(\alpha)=\mathfrak a^3\}/K^{*3}$; then $1\to E_K/E_K^3\to\mathcal V\to\mathrm{Cl}(K)[3]\to1$ is exact. By Dirichlet's unit theorem $E_K/E_K^3$ has dimension two: the cube roots of unity give a line of type $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, and the fundamental unit of $k$ gives a line of type $k$. Hence $\dim\mathcal V_k=r+1$ and $\dim\mathcal V_{k'}=s$.

steps.slogan: Compare dimensions through the inclusion of $\mathcal H$ in $\mathcal V$.
steps.detail: Since $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal V$, we have $\mathcal H_k\subseteq\mathcal V_k$, so $s\le r+1$. Also $\mathcal H_{k'}\subseteq\mathcal V_{k'}$, so $r\le s$.

concepts.c:ideal-class-group: The ranks $r$ and $s$ are ranks of 3-parts of class groups.
concepts.c:real-quadratic-field: The real field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ contributes the fundamental unit of the real subfield.
concepts.c:imaginary-quadratic-field: The imaginary field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3d})$ has only finite units.
concepts.c:cyclotomic-field: The cube roots of unity in $K$ make Kummer theory of degree three possible.

source.note: The Kummer-theory proof of Scholz's reflection principle (A. Scholz, Journal fuer die reine und angewandte Mathematik 166 (1932), 201-203), in the form of Leopoldt's reflection theorem for abelian fields.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface over $\mathbb C$ and $L$ a [nef](c:nef-line-bundle) line bundle with $L^2\ge5$. If $x$ is a base point of $|K_X+L|$, then some effective [divisor](c:divisor) $D$ through $x$ has $L\cdot D=0$ and $D^2=-1$, or $L\cdot D=1$ and $D^2=0$.

hypotheses.text: The variety $X$ is a smooth projective surface over $\mathbb C$.
The line bundle $L$ is [nef](c:nef-line-bundle) and satisfies $L^2\ge5$.
The point $x$ is a base point of $|K_X+L|$: every section of $K_X+L$ vanishes at $x$.

conclusion: There is an effective divisor $D\ni x$ with $(L\cdot D,D^2)=(0,-1)$ or $(1,0)$.

proofs.name: Serre construction and Bogomolov instability
proofs.slogan: Turn the base point into a rank-two bundle, show that it is Bogomolov unstable, and read the divisor from the destabilizing subbundle.
proofs.scope: The global generation half of Reider's theorem. The very ample half, for $L^2\ge10$ with a longer list of exceptional divisors, uses the same route with a length-two subscheme.

roles.why: On a smooth projective surface, Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing, Serre duality and the Hodge index theorem all apply.
Nefness and $L^2>0$ give vanishing of $H^1(K_X+L)$ and the inequalities of the Hodge index theorem.
The base point makes the extension class nonzero and gives the Cayley-Bacharach condition.

steps.slogan: Show that the base point gives a nonzero class in $H^1(I_x\otimes(K_X+L))$.
steps.detail: Since $L$ is nef and big, Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing gives $H^1(K_X+L)=0$. Every section vanishes at $x$, so the sequence $H^0(K_X+L)\to\mathbb C_x\to H^1(I_x(K_X+L))\to H^1(K_X+L)$ gives $H^1(I_x(K_X+L))\cong\mathbb C$.

steps.slogan: Build a rank-two [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$ by the Serre construction.
steps.detail: By Serre duality, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(I_x\otimes L,\mathcal O)\cong H^1(I_x\otimes(K_X+L))^\vee\neq0$. A nonzero class gives $0\to\mathcal O\to E\to I_x\otimes L\to0$. The base point condition is the Cayley-Bacharach condition, so $E$ is locally free with $c_1(E)=L$ and $c_2(E)=1$ (see [Chern classes](c:chern-class)).

steps.slogan: Show that $E$ is Bogomolov unstable.
steps.detail: Here $c_1(E)^2-4c_2(E)=L^2-4>0$. Bogomolov's theorem gives a saturated subsheaf $\mathcal O(M)\subset E$ with $(2M-L)^2>0$ and $(2M-L)\cdot H>0$ for an ample $H$. The quotient is $I_W(L-M)$ for a zero-dimensional $W$.

steps.slogan: Extract the effective [divisor](c:divisor) $D=L-M$ through $x$.
steps.detail: The map $\mathcal O(M)\to E\to I_x\otimes L$ is nonzero, since $M\cdot H>\tfrac12L\cdot H>0$ keeps $\mathcal O(M)$ out of $\mathcal O$. It is a section of $L-M$ that vanishes at $x$, so $D=L-M$ is effective and contains $x$. Also $1=c_2(E)=M\cdot D+\mathrm{length}(W)$ gives $L\cdot D-D^2\le1$.

steps.slogan: Bound $L\cdot D$ with the Hodge index theorem.
steps.detail: The class $L-2D=2M-L$ lies in the positive cone and $L$ is nef, so $L\cdot(L-2D)>0$ and $a=L\cdot D<L^2/2$. If $a\ge2$, then $D^2\ge a-1\ge1$ and the Hodge index theorem gives $L^2\le a^2/D^2\le a^2/(a-1)$, which contradicts $L^2>2a$. So $a\in\{0,1\}$.

steps.slogan: Read off the two cases for $(L\cdot D,D^2)$.
steps.detail: If $a=0$, the Hodge index theorem gives $D^2<0$ because $D$ is nonzero and effective, and $L\cdot D-D^2\le1$ gives $D^2\ge-1$, so $D^2=-1$. If $a=1$, then $D^2\ge0$ and $L^2D^2\le1$ with $L^2\ge5$ force $D^2=0$.

concepts.c:nef-line-bundle: Nefness gives vanishing and the sign of $L\cdot D$.
concepts.c:divisor: The conclusion is an effective divisor through the base point.
concepts.c:vector-bundle: The Serre construction turns the base point into a rank-two bundle.
concepts.c:chern-class: The Chern classes of $E$ feed the Bogomolov inequality.

source.ref: I. Reider, Vector bundles of rank 2 and linear systems on algebraic surfaces, Annals of Mathematics 127 (1988), 309-316
source.note: The steps follow Reider's argument: vanishing, Serre construction, Bogomolov's instability theorem and the Hodge index theorem.

statement: Let $D$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold), $F\subset D$ an analytic subset of dimension less than $k$, and $M$ an [analytic set](c:analytic-set) in $D\setminus F$ whose irreducible components all have dimension at least $k$. Then the [closure](c:closure) of $M$ in $D$ is an analytic subset of $D$.

hypotheses.text: The space $D$ is a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold).
The set $F\subset D$ is analytic with $\dim F<k$.
The set $M$ is an [analytic set](c:analytic-set) in $D\setminus F$, closed there, and each irreducible component of $M$ has dimension at least $k$.

conclusion: The closure of $M$ in $D$ is an analytic subset of $D$.

proofs.name: Analytic cover over a projection
proofs.slogan: Near a point of $F$, view $M$ as a finite analytic cover over a generic projection and extend the cover across the thin image of $F$.
proofs.scope: The closure is taken in $D$ and may meet $F$ in a proper analytic subset. The proof is an outline that follows the standard analytic-cover argument.

roles.why: Local holomorphic coordinates pose the problem in an open set of $\mathbb C^n$.
Since $\dim F<k$, a generic plane meets $F$ in one point and the projection of $F$ is nowhere dense.
Components of dimension at least $k$ give pure pieces with finite fibres over the projection.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a set of pure dimension $k$ near a point of $F$.
steps.detail: The set $M$ is the union of the analytic sets $M_j$ of its components of dimension $j\ge k$, and $\dim F<j$, so we treat each $M_j$ with $k$ replaced by $j$. Away from $F$ the closure equals $M$, so fix $z\in F$ and holomorphic coordinates in $\mathbb C^n$.

steps.slogan: Choose a cylinder around $z$ that meets $F$ only over a thin set.
steps.detail: Take coordinates $(w,u)\in\mathbb C^k\times\mathbb C^{n-k}$ so that the plane $\{w=0\}$ meets $F$ only at $z$ and meets $M$ in a discrete set; this is possible because $\dim F<k$. Pick $r$ so that $\{w=0,|u|=r\}$ misses $F$ and $M$, and shrink $\delta$. In the cylinder $Z=\{|w|<\delta,|u|<r\}$ the image $\pi(F\cap Z)$ under $\pi(w,u)=w$ is analytic of dimension below $k$, so it is nowhere dense.

steps.slogan: Show that $M\cap Z$ is a finite [branched cover](c:branched-cover) away from $\pi(F)$.
steps.detail: Over $\{|w|<\delta\}\setminus\pi(F)$ the map $\pi$ is proper on $M\cap Z$: limits cannot reach $|u|=r$ and cannot reach $F$. Its fibres are compact analytic subsets of a ball, so they are finite. A proper finite map from a pure $k$-dimensional set is a branched cover of constant degree.

steps.slogan: Extend the sheet functions across $\pi(F)$ by the Riemann extension theorem.
steps.detail: The symmetric functions of the sheet coordinates are holomorphic on the base minus $\pi(F)$ and are [bounded holomorphic functions](c:bounded-holomorphic-function), since $|u|<r$. By Riemann's removable singularity theorem they extend holomorphically over the nowhere dense analytic set $\pi(F)$.

steps.slogan: Identify the closure of $M\cap Z$ with the extended cover.
steps.detail: The extended functions define an analytic cover over all of $\{|w|<\delta\}$. Its total space is an analytic subset of $Z$ and equals the closure of $M\cap Z$, so the closure of $M$ is analytic near $z$. Since $z$ was arbitrary, it is analytic in $D$.

concepts.c:complex-manifold: Local coordinates reduce the claim to open sets of complex space.
concepts.c:analytic-set: Both $M$ and its closure are analytic sets.
concepts.c:closure: The theorem says that the closure of $M$ in $D$ is analytic.
concepts.c:branched-cover: Away from $\pi(F)$ the set $M$ is a finite branched cover of the base.
concepts.c:bounded-holomorphic-function: Bounded sheet functions extend across the thin set by Riemann's theorem.

source.ref: R. Remmert and K. Stein, Ueber die wesentlichen Singularitaeten analytischer Mengen, Mathematische Annalen 126 (1953), 263-306
source.note: The steps outline the standard analytic-cover argument; the cited paper contains the original proof, and Grauert and Remmert, Coherent Analytic Sheaves (1984), give a textbook account.

statement: In [absolute geometry](c:absolute-geometry) with the [Archimedean axiom](c:archimedean-axiom), the angles of a [triangle](c:triangle) add up to at most $180^\circ$.

hypotheses.text: The plane satisfies the axioms of [absolute geometry](c:absolute-geometry): incidence, order and congruence, without the parallel postulate.
The [Archimedean axiom](c:archimedean-axiom) holds.
The figure $ABC$ is a [triangle](c:triangle).

conclusion: The sum of the three [angles](c:angle) of $ABC$ is at most $180^\circ$.

proofs.name: Halving the angle
proofs.slogan: Reflect the triangle through a midpoint again and again to get a triangle with the same angle sum and a tiny angle.
proofs.scope: All triangles. The proof assumes that the angle sum exceeds $180^\circ$ and derives a contradiction; without the Archimedean axiom the theorem fails.

roles.why: Congruence of triangles and the exterior angle theorem hold without the parallel postulate.
Repeated halving of an angle makes it smaller than any given positive angle.
The triangle $ABC$ is the starting figure with the angle $\alpha$ at $A$.

steps.slogan: Assume that the angle sum of $ABC$ is $180^\circ+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$.
steps.detail: Suppose the sum of the [angles](c:angle) of $ABC$ exceeds $180^\circ$ and put $\varepsilon$ equal to the excess. Let $\alpha$ be the angle at $A$. The next steps build a triangle with the same sum and a very small angle.

steps.slogan: Reflect the triangle through the midpoint of a side to get a triangle with the same angle sum.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $E$ the point on ray $AM$ with $ME=AM$. Triangles $ABM$ and $ECM$ are congruent by SAS, since the angles at $M$ are vertical. So triangle $ACE$ has the same angle sum as $ABC$, and its angles at $A$ and $E$ add up to $\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the doubling to get a triangle with a tiny angle and the same sum.
steps.detail: One of the angles at $A$ and $E$ is at most $\alpha/2$. Repeating the step $n$ times gives a triangle with angle sum $180^\circ+\varepsilon$ and an angle of at most $\alpha/2^n$. The Archimedean property gives an $n$ with $\alpha/2^n<\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Show that two angles of any triangle add up to less than $180^\circ$.
steps.detail: The exterior angle at a vertex is larger than each remote interior angle, and this holds in absolute geometry. The exterior and interior angles at the vertex add up to $180^\circ$, so two interior angles add up to less than $180^\circ$.

steps.slogan: Add the angles of the small triangle and contradict the assumed sum.
steps.detail: In the last triangle, two angles add up to less than $180^\circ$ and the third is less than $\varepsilon$. So the sum is less than $180^\circ+\varepsilon$, which contradicts the sum $180^\circ+\varepsilon$. Hence the angle sum of $ABC$ is at most $180^\circ$.

concepts.c:absolute-geometry: Only incidence, order and congruence are allowed in the proof.
concepts.c:archimedean-axiom: It lets repeated halving of an angle go below any positive angle.
concepts.c:triangle: The theorem and the whole construction concern triangles.
concepts.c:angle: The proof tracks the sum of the angles through each reflection.

source.note: Legendre's halving proof of the Saccheri-Legendre theorem, as in M. J. Greenberg, Euclidean and Non-Euclidean Geometries, in the chapter on neutral geometry.

statement: Let $P\to M$ and $\hat P\to M$ be principal $SU(2)$-[bundles](c:principal-bundle) with 7-cocycles $H$ on $P$ and $\hat H$ on $\hat P$ that are spherical [T-dual](c:t-duality). Then the 7-[twisted cohomologies](c:twisted-cohomology) of $P$ and $\hat P$ are isomorphic by a degree-shifting isomorphism.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $P\to M$ and $\hat P\to M$ are principal $SU(2)$-[bundles](c:principal-bundle) over the same base $M$.
The classes $H\in H^7(P)$ and $\hat H\in H^7(\hat P)$ are 7-cocycles.
The pairs $(P,H)$ and $(\hat P,\hat H)$ are spherical [T-dual](c:t-duality): $p_*H=c_2(\hat P)$, $\hat p_*\hat H=c_2(P)$, and $H$, $\hat H$ pull back to compatible classes on $P\times_M\hat P$.

conclusion: There is a degree-shifting isomorphism between the 7-[twisted cohomology](c:twisted-cohomology) of $P$ and that of $\hat P$.

proofs.name: Correspondence space and spectral sequences
proofs.slogan: Pass to the correspondence space, build a pull-push transform with the common twist, and check it on spectral sequences where duality swaps the two differentials.
proofs.scope: The isomorphism of 7-twisted cohomologies for every dual pair. The integral version needs $\dim M\le7$, the twisted K-theory version needs $\dim M\le4$, and the existence of duals is a separate question.

roles.why: Both bundles have fibre $S^3$, so the correspondence space is a bundle over each of them.
The classes $H$ and $\hat H$ define the twisted differentials on the two cohomologies.
The duality relations swap the roles of $H$ and the Chern class in the two bundles.

steps.slogan: Form the correspondence space of the two bundles over $M$.
steps.detail: Let $Q=P\times_M\hat P$ with projections $\pi\colon Q\to P$ and $\hat\pi\colon Q\to\hat P$. Each projection is a bundle with fibre the [3-sphere](c:3-sphere), because it is the pullback of the other principal bundle.

steps.slogan: Use the duality conditions to put one twisting class on $Q$.
steps.detail: The classes $\pi^*H$ and $\hat\pi^*\hat H$ in $H^7(Q)$ are compatible. A choice of trivialization of their difference identifies the twisted complex of $\pi^*H$ with that of $\hat\pi^*\hat H$ on $Q$.

steps.slogan: Define the transform by pull-back, a kernel class and fibre integration.
steps.detail: Set $\Phi(\omega)=\hat\pi_*(K\cup\pi^*\omega)$, where $K$ is a kernel class on $Q$ built from the trivialization. Integration over the fibres of $\hat\pi$ lowers the degree, which gives the degree shift.

steps.slogan: Check that the transform commutes with the twisted differentials.
steps.detail: Pull-back commutes with the twisted differential $d+H\wedge$ by naturality. The duality relations $p_*H=c_2(\hat P)$ and $\hat p_*\hat H=c_2(P)$ make the kernel compatible with both twisted differentials, so $\Phi$ is a chain map.

steps.slogan: Show that the transform is an isomorphism by comparing the Leray-Serre spectral sequences.
steps.detail: In the spectral sequence of an $S^3$-bundle, the first differential on the fibre class is the product with $c_2$, and the twist adds the term $p_*H$. Duality swaps these two data between $P$ and $\hat P$, so $\Phi$ matches the pages up to the shift and is an isomorphism on cohomology.

concepts.c:principal-bundle: The two spaces are principal bundles over the same base.
concepts.c:t-duality: Spherical T-duality swaps the 7-class with the Chern class.
concepts.c:twisted-cohomology: The isomorphism is between the twisted cohomologies of the two total spaces.
concepts.c:3-sphere: The fibre of both bundles is the 3-sphere, which sets the degree shift.

source.ref: P. Bouwknegt, J. Evslin and V. Mathai, Spherical T-duality, Communications in Mathematical Physics (2015), arXiv:1405.5844
source.note: The steps outline the cited proof that every spherical T-duality induces a degree-shifting isomorphism of 7-twisted cohomologies; exact formulas are in the paper.

statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices with $B$ [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix). Then the [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) of the [matrix exponential](c:matrix-exponential) $e^{A-tB}$ is a [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) of a positive measure: $\operatorname{tr}e^{A-tB}=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-ts}\,d\mu(s)$ for $t\ge0$.

hypotheses.text: The matrices $A$ and $B$ are Hermitian of size $n\times n$.
The matrix $B$ is [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix).

conclusion: There is a positive finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $\operatorname{tr}e^{A-tB}=\int e^{-ts}\,d\mu(s)$ for all $t\ge0$.

proofs.name: Riemann surface of the eigenvalues
proofs.slogan: Write the trace through the eigenvalue branches on a Riemann surface, represent it as a Laplace transform, and show that the measure is positive.
proofs.scope: All Hermitian $A$ and positive semidefinite $B$. The proof is an outline of Stahl's argument in Eremenko's simplified account.

roles.why: Hermitian pencils have real analytic eigenvalue branches and a symmetric surface, which fix the sign of the density.
Since $B\ge0$ the trace stays bounded for $t\ge0$, which puts the measure on $[0,\infty)$.

steps.slogan: Write the trace as a sum over the [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) branches of $A-tB$.
steps.detail: The trace is $f(t)=\sum_j e^{\lambda_j(t)}$, where $\lambda_j(t)$ are the eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix $A-tB$. By Rellich's theorem they are real analytic in $t$, and $\lambda_j(t)=-b_jt+O(1)$ as $t\to\infty$, where $b_j$ are the eigenvalues of $B$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) of the [algebraic function](c:algebraic-function) $\lambda(t)$.
steps.detail: The values $\lambda_j(t)$ solve the polynomial equation $\det(\lambda I-A+tB)=0$ in $t$ and $\lambda$. They are the branches of one algebraic function on a surface with $n$ sheets over the sphere, which is unramified over a region that contains the real line and a neighborhood of infinity.

steps.slogan: Represent $f$ as a Laplace transform of a real measure built on the surface.
steps.detail: Stahl writes $f(t)=\int e^{-ts}\,d\mu(s)$ for a real measure $\mu$ whose density comes from boundary values of the branches along curves on the surface. The sum over the sheets of the surface gives the sum over $j$.

steps.slogan: Prove that the density of $\mu$ is non-negative.
steps.detail: This is the main step. Stahl studies the geometry of the Riemann surface and shows that the contributions of the sheets to the density have a definite sign. The Hermitian symmetry of $A$ and $B$ enters here.

steps.slogan: Use $B\ge0$ to place the measure on $[0,\infty)$ with finite mass.
steps.detail: For $t\ge0$ the Golden-Thompson inequality gives $f(t)\le\operatorname{tr}(e^Ae^{-tB})\le\operatorname{tr}e^A$, since $e^{-tB}\le I$. A positive measure whose Laplace transform stays bounded as $t\to\infty$ lives on $[0,\infty)$, and its total mass is $f(0)=\operatorname{tr}e^A$.

concepts.c:positive-semidefinite-matrix: The condition $B\ge0$ keeps the trace bounded and the measure on the half line.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: The theorem concerns the trace of the exponential.
concepts.c:laplace-transform: The trace is shown to be the Laplace transform of a positive measure.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The trace is the sum of exponentials of the eigenvalues of $A-tB$.
concepts.c:riemann-surface: The eigenvalue branches live on one Riemann surface with $n$ sheets.
concepts.c:algebraic-function: The eigenvalues of $A-tB$ form one algebraic function of $t$.

source.ref: H. R. Stahl, Proof of the BMV conjecture, Acta Mathematica 211 (2013), 255-290
source.note: The steps outline Stahl's proof in the simplified account of A. Eremenko, Herbert Stahl's proof of the BMV conjecture, arXiv:1312.6003.

statement: Let $X$ be a closed [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) and $V\to X$ a real [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $d$, with fiberwise [one-point compactification](c:one-point-compactification) $S^V$. Homotopy classes of sections of $S^V$, the twisted [cohomotopy](c:twisted-cohomotopy) of $X$, match [cobordism](c:cobordism) classes of closed codimension-$d$ submanifolds $\Sigma\subset X$ with an isomorphism $\nu_\Sigma\cong V|_\Sigma$ of the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a closed (compact, boundaryless) [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold).
The twist is a real [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $V\to X$ of rank $d$, through its sphere bundle $S^V$.

conclusion: The map $s\mapsto(s^{-1}(0),ds)$ is a bijection from homotopy classes of sections of $S^V$ to $V$-framed cobordism classes in $X$.

proofs.name: Transversality and collapse
proofs.slogan: Make sections transverse to the zero section, read off the framed zero set, and invert the map by the Pontryagin-Thom collapse.
proofs.scope: The theorem for a vector bundle twist on a closed manifold; for $V$ trivial it is Pontryagin's theorem. Cobordism means a $V$-framed submanifold of $X\times[0,1]$ that meets the ends transversally.

roles.why: Compactness makes zero sets closed submanifolds, and tubular neighborhoods exist.
The zero section and the vertical derivative of a section use the vector bundle structure.

steps.slogan: Perturb a section until it is [transverse](c:transversality) to the zero section.
steps.detail: By Thom's transversality theorem every section $s$ of $S^V$ is homotopic to one transverse to the zero section. Then $\Sigma=s^{-1}(0)$ is a closed submanifold of codimension $d$, and the vertical derivative of $s$ is an isomorphism $\nu_\Sigma\to V|_\Sigma$.

steps.slogan: Show that homotopic sections give cobordant framed submanifolds.
steps.detail: A homotopy of sections, made transverse relative to its ends, is a section over $X\times[0,1]$. Its zero set $W$ is a submanifold with the derivative framing, and it is a cobordism between the two zero sets.

steps.slogan: Build a section from a framed submanifold by the Pontryagin-Thom collapse.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi\colon\nu_\Sigma\to V|_\Sigma$ be the framing and let $U$ be a [tubular neighborhood](c:tubular-neighborhood) of $\Sigma$. Send $\exp_x(v)$ with $|v|<1$ to $\varphi(v)/(1-|v|^2)\in V_x$, and send every point outside $U$ to $\infty$. This is the construction of Pontryagin's theorem with the twist $V$.

steps.slogan: Show that cobordant framed submanifolds give homotopic sections.
steps.detail: Apply the same construction to a $V$-framed cobordism $W\subset X\times[0,1]$. It gives a section over $X\times[0,1]$ whose restrictions to the two ends are the sections built from the two submanifolds, so these sections are homotopic.

steps.slogan: Check that the two constructions are inverse to each other.
steps.detail: If $s$ is transverse with zero set $\Sigma$ and derivative $\varphi$, a straight-line homotopy in $V$ near $\Sigma$ and a stretch to $\infty$ elsewhere joins $s$ to the collapse section of $(\Sigma,\varphi)$. Conversely, the collapse section of $(\Sigma,\varphi)$ is transverse with zero set $\Sigma$ and derivative $\varphi$.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Transversality and tubular neighborhoods need the smooth structure of $X$.
concepts.c:vector-bundle: The twist is a vector bundle with a zero section and vertical derivative.
concepts.c:one-point-compactification: A point at infinity in each fibre makes $S^V$ a bundle with compact fibres.
concepts.c:twisted-cohomotopy: Homotopy classes of sections of $S^V$ are the twisted cohomotopy set.
concepts.c:cobordism: The target of the bijection is a set of framed cobordism classes.
concepts.c:normal-bundle: The framing identifies the normal bundle of the submanifold with $V$.
concepts.c:transversality: Transversality makes the zero set a submanifold and gives its framing.
concepts.c:tubular-neighborhood: The tubular neighborhood carries the section built from a framed submanifold.

source.note: The Pontryagin-Thom construction with a vector bundle twist; Milnor, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, section 7, treats the untwisted case.
